1. MODEL INTRODUCTION   *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-1-model-introduction*

Muse Glimmer is a multimodal reasoning model. You can serve Muse Glimmer in
four formats:

- A BF16 checkpoint (`MuseGlimmerForConditionalGeneration`).
- A set of vendor GGUF files.
- A ready-to-serve NVFP4 + MXFP8 checkpoint.
- Three MLX repacks for Apple Silicon.

Form                Source                        Notes
------------------  ----------------------------  ----------------------------
BF16                meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B  Supports image input.
GGUF Q4_K_M         meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-     Text only. This path is not
                    30B-GGUF                      optimized. SGLang shows a
                                                  warning at startup.
NVFP4               RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-NVFP4   Text only. Ready to serve,
                                                  no conversion needed.
MLX Q4              RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4-MLX  Text only. Apple Silicon
                                                  (MLX backend). Same serve
                                                  recipe as gs128, no measured
                                                  round yet. See §3.4.
MLX Q4_K_M (gs128)  RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4km-   Text only. Apple Silicon
                    gs128-MLX                     (MLX backend). Carries the
                                                  vendor GGUF's exact
                                                  quantization codes in MLX
                                                  format. The measured MLX
                                                  artifact. See §3.4.
MLX Q4_K (dynamic)  RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4k-    Text only. Apple Silicon
                    dynamic-MLX                   (MLX backend). Same serve
                                                  recipe as gs128, no measured
                                                  round yet. See §3.4.

Resources: Muse-Glimmer-30B (BF16)
https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B ·
Muse-Glimmer-30B-assistant (DFlash draft)
https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-assistant ·
Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF
https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF ·
Muse-Glimmer-NVFP4 https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-NVFP4 · MLX
· q4 https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4-MLX · q4km-gs128
https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4km-gs128-MLX · q4k-dynamic
https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4k-dynamic-MLX.

2. CONFIGURATION TIPS   *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-2-configuration-tips*

The GGUF format is text only. SGLang has no `mmproj` path. You cannot use
the vision GGUF files. Use the BF16 checkpoint for multimodal input.

The NVFP4 checkpoint. `RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-NVFP4` is a ready-to-serve
NVFP4 + MXFP8 checkpoint. No conversion needed --- point `--model-path`
straight at it.

The DFlash draft. `meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-assistant` is the vendor's
native draft export and serves directly. No conversion needed.

DFlash with a GGUF target model needs
`--speculative-draft-load-format auto`. Without this flag, the draft model
uses the `gguf` load format from the target model. The loader then rejects
the draft directory.

Apple Silicon uses an MLX checkpoint, not the GGUF files. The MLX backend
has no GGUF path. Serve one of the three `RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-*-MLX`
artifacts with `SGLANG_USE_MLX=1` (see the Apple Silicon cells in the
command panel). All three take the same flags; `q4km-gs128` is the one with
a measured round. Keep `--disable-radix-cache` --- the windowed KV storage
for the sliding-window layers requires it --- and set
`SGLANG_MLX_CACHE_LIMIT_GB=8` so the MLX buffer cache does not grow the
footprint under concurrent load. Speculative decoding is not available on
the MLX backend.

3. ADVANCED USAGE           *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-3-advanced-usage*

3.1 Reasoning                  *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-3-1-reasoning*

Muse Glimmer enables the `muse` reasoning parser by default. This parser
separates the reasoning text from the final answer.

                    *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-reasoning-example-python*
Reasoning Example (Python)

  [Example]

  [Example]Example

  >python
      from openai import OpenAI

      client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")
      resp = client.chat.completions.create(
          model="meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B",
          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is 15% of 240?"}],
      )
      msg = resp.choices[0].message
      print("Reasoning:", getattr(msg, "reasoning_content", None))
      print("Answer:", msg.content)
<

3.2 Tool Calling            *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-3-2-tool-calling*

Muse Glimmer enables the `muse` tool-call parser by default. This parser
sends structured tool calls in `message.tool_calls`.

3.3 Multimodal                *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-3-3-multimodal*

The BF16 checkpoint supports image input. It defaults to text only. To
switch, select Modality in the command panel above.

Text only adds `--language-model-only`. This flag turns off the vision
tower. SGLang does not build or load the vision weights. This frees memory
for the KV cache. SGLang rejects image requests in this mode.

Select Image + text to turn on image input.

NVFP4, GGUF, and the MLX artifacts are text only. The Modality option does
not appear for GGUF or MLX; NVFP4 only offers Text only.

                       *autoregressive-Meta-MuseGlimmer-3-4-apple-silicon-mlx*
3.4 Apple Silicon (MLX)

The MLX backend serves three Muse Glimmer artifacts on Apple Silicon Macs
(48 GB unified memory or more). All three are text only --- the MLX backend
has no vision path --- and all three take the same flags, so pick one in the
command panel:

- `RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4-MLX` --- no measured round yet.
- `RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4km-gs128-MLX` --- a lossless repack of the
  vendor's Q4_K_M (gs128) GGUF: every weight keeps the GGUF's exact
  quantization code, with the group scales re-expressed in MLX affine bf16
  (≤2⁻⁸ relative rounding). The numbers below are for this artifact.
- `RadixArk/Muse-Glimmer-q4k-dynamic-MLX` --- no measured round yet.

Choose along the speed-versus-accuracy axis: footprint and expected accuracy
both grow `q4` → `q4km-gs128` → `q4k-dynamic`, and decode speed moves the
other way. Decode on Apple Silicon is memory-bandwidth-bound, so a smaller
artifact reads fewer weight bytes per token --- more tokens per second, and
more unified memory left over for the KV cache. Take `q4` for the fastest
responses on the smallest machine, `q4k-dynamic` to stay closest to BF16,
and `q4km-gs128` for the middle ground --- it is also the only one of the
three with a measured round, below.

This table shows accuracy for the gs128 checkpoint, with the vendor
llama.cpp fork serving the source GGUF on the same machine as the reference.
GSM8K: 200 questions, no-thinking chat template, temperature 0, max 2048 new
tokens. CIMemories: 1 profile, full combo, single trial, DeepSeek-R1-0528
judge.

Benchmark                                    SGLang MLX  llama.cpp (same GGUF)
-------------------------------------------  ----------  ---------------------
GSM8K (200q, no-thinking, greedy)            0.970       0.970
CIMemories --- violation rate (lower is        0.00%       8.27%
better)
CIMemories --- coverage (higher is better)     76.0%       68.4%

CIMemories is a single-trial benchmark with a nondeterministic judge; treat
the SGLang-vs-llama.cpp gap on that row as run noise, not a runtime effect.
GSM8K parity is exact.

Decode throughput for gs128 on an M5 Pro (64 GB), 1k-in/1k-out greedy: 15.3
tok/s at batch 1, rising to 52.6 tok/s aggregate at batch 8 --- ahead of
llama.cpp on the same GGUF codes at every batch size above 1.

Muse Spark Open                     *sglang-autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen*

Deploy Muse Spark Open with SGLang --- launch recipes, feature
compatibility, and tuning notes for GB300, B300, B200, H200, MI355X, Intel
Xeon

DEPLOYMENT                      *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-deployment*

Install SGLang              *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-install-sglang*

  [Command]

  [Command]Command

  >bash
      docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:latest                # NVIDIA B300 / GB300 / B200 / H200
      docker pull lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:muse-spark-open    # AMD MI355X
      docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dev-muse-spark-xeon     # Intel Xeon CPU
<
  The deployment panel can render a complete `docker run` command for the
  selected hardware and options. See
  |docs-get-started-install-method-3-using-docker| for host setup. The CUDA
  tag does not run on MI355X; use the ROCm image there; Use Xeon image for
  Xeon CPU and for more SGLang CPU installation approaches, see the
  |docs-hardware-platforms-cpu_server-installation|.

Choose your Hardware Platform, Strategy, and Quantization below. The default
is B300 / Low Latency / NVFP4. Low Latency keeps unified memory disabled;
High Throughput removes all speculative decoding parameters and enables
unified memory on NVIDIA GPUs (B300, GB300, B200, and H200). On TPU v7 (one
host, SGLang-TorchTPU https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu), Low
Latency keeps DFlash at 2 running requests and High Throughput runs 64
requests without speculative decoding. TPU v7 support is not merged yet: it
runs from the SGLang-TorchTPU branch `haolin/ms-v11`
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu/tree/haolin/ms-v11, which we
are actively upstreaming. Its commands still carry many TPU-specific
settings; we will productionize TPU v7 support and remove most of them. Use
the Playground to tune parallelism, caching, speculative decoding,
multimodal transport, and prefill/decode disaggregation.

With a current SGLang build, the commands omit settings inferred from the
checkpoint and GPU. Muse Spark NVFP4 selects `modelopt_fp4`, with
`flashinfer_trtllm` MoE on B200/B300/GB300 or `marlin` on H200. The default
static memory fraction is `0.8` on Blackwell and `0.85` on Hopper; recipes
with a different budget keep an explicit override. LayerNorm-SP enables
MegaMoE automatically for NVFP4 on data-center Blackwell when EP equals TP
and is greater than 1, except on PD decode workers. Use
`--no-enable-megamoe-for-layernorm-sp` to opt out. Muse Spark DFlash2 drafts
default to FA4 on these NVIDIA platforms and eight draft tokens. Explicit
settings take precedence.

PLAYGROUND                      *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground*

The Playground is where you experiment with SGLang features beyond the
verified matrix. The Deploy panel above only emits combinations the SGLang
team has signed off on; the Playground lets you turn on additional knobs on
top of whichever cell the Deploy panel is currently showing.

The Unified Memory control has Enable and Disable options. It initially
inherits the current Deployment command and resets to that command when you
change the Deployment selection. Enable is unavailable on MI355X and Xeon
because their `aiter` and `intel_amx` attention backends do not support the
unified KV layout.

           *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-agentic-long-context-deployment*
AGENTIC LONG-CONTEXT DEPLOYMENT

Agentic workloads, such as coding agents and other multi-turn, tool-using
assistants, send long prompts whose prefixes grow and repeat from turn to
turn. Serving them well depends on reusing the KV cache across turns,
offloading it beyond GPU memory, and keeping each session on the workers
that already hold its prefix. This section gives complete launch commands
for such deployments, each benchmarked in SemiAnalysis InferenceX
https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/ and linked to the run that measured it.
Pick a hardware platform, checkpoint, deployment shape, concurrency, KV
cache offloading mechanism and router to get every process of the deployment
as a raw command, one tab per process in launch order.

- Router. Each configuration was submitted behind one front door: Dynamo
  (`dynamo.frontend` with `dynamo.sglang` workers) or SGLang
  (`sglang.launch_server`, behind a router when there are several workers or
  DP-attention ranks).
- KV offload. Choose among these KV cache offloading mechanisms: none (GPU
  KV only), HiCache (host DRAM), or a Mooncake store attached through the
  external linker. The Mooncake option needs an image whose SGLang build
  includes `--enable-unified-cache-external-linker`.
- Container image. Run the commands inside the image listed for each
  configuration; flag names follow that image.

*autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-gb300-deployments-measured-with-artificial-analysis-agentperf*
GB300 deployments measured with Artificial Analysis AgentPerf

Five aggregated Dynamo + SGLang deployments on GB300, measured with the
Artificial Analysis AgentPerf
https://github.com/ArtificialAnalysis/agentperf-client coding-agent
workload. Together they span the trade-off from the lowest per-user latency
(concurrency 1) to the highest throughput per GPU (concurrency 160), ordered
from low latency to high throughput. Each one starts from the Artificial
Analysis SGLang submission for this model and changes only flags,
environment variables and parallelism.

- Container image.
  `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-muse-spark-open@sha256:8cfc5a72cb296771f5f8a4a4688cb6d05685610a830cbb616fa4ab0eb7bb2b0a`
  with the Dynamo wheels added:
  `pip install --no-deps ai-dynamo==1.6.0.dev20261019 ai-dynamo-runtime==1.6.0.dev20261019`.
- Router. One Dynamo frontend with the KV-aware router. Session affinity
  keeps requests that carry the same `X-Dynamo-Session-ID` header on one
  worker; the AgentPerf client sends one ID per agent session.
- Checkpoints. `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4` with the
  DFlash2 draft `RadixArk/Muse-Spark-Open-DFlash2` (8 draft tokens, FP8 KV
  cache).
- HiCache. `--hicache-size` is the host tier in GB per rank; scale it to
  your host memory.
- Two-node deployments. The TP8·EP8 worker spans two GB300 trays (4 GPUs
  each) over multi-node NVLink: run the worker command on both nodes, with
  `NODE_RANK` 0 on the first.

*autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-agg-tp8ep8-2-nodes-lowest-latency-8-gpus-concurrency-1*
Agg TP8·EP8 (2 nodes), lowest latency · 8 GPUs · concurrency 1

  Env Vars                          *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-env-vars*

  >bash
      export ETCD_IP=<node running etcd>
      export AGG_HEAD_IP=<first node of the worker>
      export NODE_RANK=<0 on the first node, 1 on the second>

        --data-dir /tmp/etcd \
        --listen-client-urls http://0.0.0.0:2379 \

  Dynamo frontend            *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-dynamo-frontend*

  >bash
      export DYN_REQUEST_PLANE=tcp
      export DYN_ROUTER_QUEUE_THRESHOLD=None
      export DYN_ROUTER_TEMPERATURE=0
      export DYN_TOKENIZER=fastokens
      export DYN_TOKENIZER_CACHE=1
      export DYN_TOKENIZER_CACHE_BYTES=8000000000
      export ETCD_ENDPOINTS=http://$ETCD_IP:2379

      python3 -m dynamo.frontend \
        --http-port 8000 \
        --router-mode kv \
        --router-session-affinity-ttl-secs 14400 \
        --active-decode-blocks-threshold None \
        --active-prefill-tokens-threshold None \
        --active-prefill-tokens-threshold-frac None
<

  SGLang worker (run on each of the 2 nodes) *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-sglang-worker-run-on-each-of-the-2-nodes*

  >bash

        --request-plane tcp \
        --dyn-reasoning-parser muse \
        --dyn-tool-call-parser muse \
        --expert-parallel-size 8 \
        --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
        --max-running-requests 32 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
        --mm-feature-transport cpu \
        --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
        --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
        --reasoning-parser muse \
        --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
        --speculative-draft-attention-backend fa4 \
        --speculative-draft-model-path RadixArk/Muse-Spark-Open-DFlash2 \
        --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 \
        --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.1 \
        --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
        --trust-remote-code \
        --watchdog-timeout 3600

*autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-tpu-v7-deployment-measured-with-semianalysis-inferencex*
TPU v7 deployment measured with SemiAnalysis InferenceX

  Note: ~

  TPU v7 support is not merged yet. The commands below run on the
  SGLang-TorchTPU branch `haolin/ms-v11`
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu/tree/haolin/ms-v11, which
  we are actively upstreaming. They are the settings used for the InferenceX
  submission, including many experimental environment variables and flags.
  We will productionize TPU v7 support and remove most of these settings.

DFlash V2 on one Google Cloud TPU v7 host (2x2x1: 4 chips, 8 TensorCores,
`--tp-size 8`) with SGLang-TorchTPU
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu, measured in
SemiAnalysis InferenceX https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/. The run is not
public yet, so it has no link here. The explorer above is generated from
public InferenceX data only, which is why TPU v7 is listed in this
hand-written section.

- Container image. `<public sglang-torchtpu image: TBD>`.
- Host. 960 GiB of RAM. The HiCache host tier is 2.0x the device KV pool per
  rank through concurrency 10, and 56 GB per rank from concurrency 16
  (`--hicache-size 56`, 448 GB across the eight ranks).
- Acceptance. SemiAnalysis measured these points with a synthetic
  speculative-decoding acceptance length of 4.05 (InferenceX golden AL via
  `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_LEN`), which is not part of these commands. Where a
  command sets `SGLANG_TPU_DFLASH_ADAPTIVE_VERIFY=MIN_BS:4:3.06`, steps with
  at least `MIN_BS` decoding requests verify only the first 4 tokens of the
  8-token draft block, and the measurement gave those steps the golden
  acceptance length for 3 draft tokens, 3.06 (the rule's third field). The
  engine reads that field only when `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_LEN` is set. Real
  speed depends on your workload's acceptance.
- Settings. The commands are the submission's server settings, from
  `agentx.py`
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu/blob/haolin/ms-v11/benchmark/tpu/recipe/configs/muse_spark/agentx.py
  in SGLang-TorchTPU, without its logging, diagnostics and telemetry
  settings and without values equal to the engine defaults.

1. MODEL INTRODUCTION *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-1-model-introduction*

This cookbook provides deployment recipes for the Muse Spark Open 816B-A42B
checkpoints:

- NVFP4: `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4` (NVIDIA default).
- MXFP4: `amd/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-Quark-MXFP4` (MI355X default;
  Quark-quantized).
- NVFP4 on MI355X (direct load): the same
  `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4` checkpoint runs on MI355X
  with `--quantization quark_mxfp4`; the weights are requantized to MXFP4
  while loading, so no separate export is needed. Select MI355X / NVFP4 in
  the panel for this command.
- INT4 `intel-ai/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-INT4` (Xeon default;
  AutoRound-quantized).
- BF16: `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B`.

2. CONFIGURATION TIPS *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-2-configuration-tips*

H200 configuration      *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-h200-configuration*

NVFP4 runs on one 8x H200 node with Marlin W4A16 experts
(`--moe-runner-backend marlin`), since Hopper has no TRT-LLM FP4 MoE. The
BF16 checkpoint does not fit on one node, so it runs TP16/EP16 across two
nodes; replace `<node-rank>` and `<node0-ip>` for each node. Prefill
sequence parallel and MegaMoE need SM100 kernels and are unavailable on
H200.

            *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-xeon-cpu-service-configuration*
Xeon CPU service configuration

- Xeon serves the INT4 checkpoint (quantized by Intel AutoRound, HF id:
  `intel-ai/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-INT4`) on the SGLang CPU engine. A
  typical Xeon 6 P-core platform (e.g., Xeon 6980P) is recommended.
- Set `--page-size 1` for the `intel_amx` attention backend (the CPU default
  attention backend).
- We recommend setting the TP size equal to the NUMA count. See the Notes
  under |docs-hardware-platforms-cpu_server-launch-of-the-serving-engine| in
  the SGLang CPU server document for how to configure the arguments,
  especially TP and NUMA binding.

3. ADVANCED USAGE         *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-advanced-usage*

3.1 Reasoning                *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-1-reasoning*

On the server, enable `--reasoning-parser muse` in your `sglang serve`
command. The |autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-deployment| recipes above
already include this flag; in the
|autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground|, keep Reasoning Parser
enabled under Parsers. The parser separates the model's reasoning into
`message.reasoning_content` and its final answer into `message.content`.

On the client, set `reasoning_effort` for each chat completion request. Muse
Spark Open supports four levels: `low`, `medium`, `high`, and `xhigh`. If
you omit the parameter, the checkpoint's chat template defaults to `xhigh`.
Use `low` or `medium` for faster, shorter responses, and `high` or `xhigh`
for complex problem solving, coding, and agentic tasks. Other values,
including `minimal`, are not supported. See the model card
https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the
supported settings.

The example below connects to the server on port `30000` and discovers its
model ID, so it works with whichever checkpoint you selected in Deployment.
Change `base_url` if the server runs on another host or port. The current
checkpoint's chat template does not require
`chat_template_kwargs={"thinking": True}`; set the reasoning level with
`reasoning_effort`.

                  *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-reasoning-example-python*
Reasoning Example (Python)

  [Example]

  [Example]Example

  >python
      from openai import OpenAI

      client = OpenAI(
          base_url="http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1",
          api_key="EMPTY",
          timeout=600.0,
      )
      model = client.models.list().data[0].id
      response = client.chat.completions.create(
          model=model,
          messages=[
              {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Briefly explain: what is SGLang?"},
          ],
          max_tokens=16384,
          reasoning_effort="xhigh",  # low | medium | high | xhigh (default)
      )
      choice = response.choices[0]
      print("Reasoning:", getattr(choice.message, "reasoning_content", None))
      print("Content:", choice.message.content)
      print("Finish reason:", choice.finish_reason)
<

3.2 Tool calling          *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-2-tool-calling*

On the server, enable `--tool-call-parser muse` alongside
`--reasoning-parser muse` in your `sglang serve` command. The
|autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-deployment| recipes above already include
both flags; in the |autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground|, keep Tool
Call Parser and Reasoning Parser enabled under Parsers. SGLang converts Muse
Spark Open's native tool-call format into OpenAI-compatible
`message.tool_calls`, while keeping reasoning in
`message.reasoning_content`.

On the client, pass function definitions in `tools`, with each function's
arguments described by a JSON Schema. The checkpoint's chat template
https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4/blob/main/chat_template.jinja
formats these definitions for the model. With `tool_choice="auto"`, the
model decides whether to call a tool. The example below requests a weather
lookup and prints each returned function name and its JSON arguments.

               *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-tool-calling-example-python*
Tool Calling Example (Python)

  [Example]

  [Example]Example

  >python
      import json

      from openai import OpenAI

      client = OpenAI(
          base_url="http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1",
          api_key="EMPTY",
          timeout=600.0,
      )
      model = client.models.list().data[0].id

      tools = [
          {
              "type": "function",
              "function": {
                  "name": "get_weather",
                  "description": "Get the current weather for a city.",
                  "parameters": {
                      "type": "object",
                      "properties": {
                          "location": {
                              "type": "string",
                              "description": "City name, for example Beijing.",
                          },
                          "unit": {
                              "type": "string",
                              "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                          },
                      },
                      "required": ["location", "unit"],
                      "additionalProperties": False,
                  },
              },
          }
      ]

      response = client.chat.completions.create(
          model=model,
          messages=[
              {"role": "user", "content": "Use get_weather to check the current weather in Beijing in Celsius."},
          ],
          tools=tools,
          tool_choice="auto",
          reasoning_effort="xhigh",
          max_tokens=16384,
      )
      choice = response.choices[0]
      message = choice.message
      print("Reasoning:", getattr(message, "reasoning_content", None))
      print("Content:", message.content)
      for tool_call in message.tool_calls or []:
          print("Tool call ID:", tool_call.id)
          print("Function:", tool_call.function.name)
          print("Arguments:", json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments))
      print("Finish reason:", choice.finish_reason)
<

This example inspects the requested tool calls; it does not fetch weather

  *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-3-encode-prefill-decode-disaggregation*
3.3 Encode Prefill Decode Disaggregation

Encoder--Prefill--Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates media encoding,
prompt processing, and token generation, so encoding-heavy image/video
requests can be scheduled separately from language inference. The encoder
sends features through `zmq_to_tokenizer`; prefill transfers KV state to
decode through Mooncake, with a router exposing one client endpoint.

The examples below use one 8× B300 NVLink host: encoder TP2 shares GPUs 0--1
with prefill TP4/EP4 on GPUs 0--3; decode TP4/EP4 uses GPUs 4--7. Run each
command in a separate shell using the NVIDIA image from
|autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-deployment|, with a shared host network.
Start encoder, prefill, decode, then router, waiting for each to become
ready. Prefill (`30001`), decode (`30002`), and router (`8000`) match the
Playground ports; the encoder uses `30010`.

  Note: ~

  These are simplified examples derived from PR #265
  https://github.com/radixark/sglang-muse-spark/pull/265. The source run
  checked transport with simulated outputs; this ordinary-serving
  configuration still needs runtime and accuracy validation. Leave GPU
  memory headroom for the encoder sharing the prefill GPUs.

              *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-encoder-server-b300-gpus-0-1*
Encoder server (B300, GPUs 0--1)

  [Command]

  [Command]Command

  >bash
      CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 sglang serve \
        --model-path meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 \
        --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
        --tp-size 2 \
        --encoder-only \
        --encoder-transfer-backend zmq_to_tokenizer \
        --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --port 30010
<

         *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-4-sequence-parallel-for-prefill*
3.4 Sequence Parallel for Prefill

Sequence parallelism (SP) splits activations along the token dimension
across TP ranks. Each rank processes its own token shard for normalization,
pooling, and unpooling, reducing duplicated computation and activation
storage during long-prompt prefill. NVFP4 MegaMoE connects these shards to
expert parallelism through integrated all-to-all dispatch and combine:
tokens reach their selected experts, and weighted expert outputs return to
the original token ranks.

For a Blackwell NVFP4 configuration (B300, B200, or GB300), use the
|autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground| to enable Prefill Sequence
Parallel and Prefill MegaMoE together. This adds
`--enable-layernorm-sp --enable-megamoe-for-layernorm-sp` to the launch
command. Keep Attention TP and MoE EP equal; MegaMoE requires SP to remain
on. These prefill options are unavailable on H200 and are omitted for a PD
decode worker.

*autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-5-speculative-decoding-with-dflash-v2-and-block-verification*
3.5 Speculative Decoding with DFlash v2 and Block Verification

DFlash V2 uses the target model's hidden states to propose a block of future
tokens in one draft-model forward pass; Muse Spark Open then verifies the
block in a single pass, advancing by multiple tokens when proposals are
accepted. V2 mixes information across neighboring draft positions and
selects candidates with their dependencies in mind. Optional
block verification https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10444 evaluates draft prefixes
jointly instead of token by token, potentially accepting longer prefixes
while preserving the target sampling distribution.

In the |autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground|, select DFlash V2
under Speculative Decoding to add `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH` and
`--speculative-draft-model-path RadixArk/Muse-Spark-Open-DFlash2`. Then
adjust:

- Draft attention backend: `fa4` for NVIDIA or `triton` for MI355X,
  inherited from Deployment and set with
  `--speculative-draft-attention-backend`.
- Num draft tokens: 1--8, default 8, set with
  `--speculative-num-draft-tokens`.
- Block Verification: turn it on to add
  `--speculative-use-block-verification`; it is off by default.

The Deployment Low Latency strategy enables DFlash V2 on supported GPUs;
High Throughput leaves speculative decoding off. The Playground inherits
that choice and lets you override it.

   *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-3-6-megakernel-with-helion-experimental*
3.6 MegaKernel with Helion (Experimental)

We support persistent Helion megakernels for DFlash V2 target verification.
They fuse attention, projection and normalization boundaries, routing, MoE,
and the layer tail, with a separate fused LM head, reducing kernel launches
and communication overhead. TP4/EP1 shards each expert across four GPUs,
avoiding the expert-load imbalance of EP4 at batch size 1. With BS=1 +
DFlash V2, the reported decode performance is roughly 10% faster than the
TP4/EP4 baseline without megakernels on 4×GB300; gains depend on the
workload.

Use this experimental recipe only on a PD-disaggregated decode worker, with
four GB300 (SM 10.3) GPUs, NVFP4 weights, FP8 E4M3 KV cache, and
`helion==1.5.0`. Keep prefill on the regular path: EP1 prefill is slower
than the TP4/EP4 baseline. This specialized TP4/EP1 command is separate from
the Playground's equal-TP/EP configuration.

              *autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-helion-decode-worker-4-gb300*
Helion decode worker (4×GB300)

  Install the dependency in the serving environment, then launch the decode
  worker:

  [Command]

  [Command]Command

  >bash
      python -m pip install helion==1.5.0

      export NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1
      export NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=1
      export NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1
      export SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL=NVLINK
      export MC_FORCE_MNNVL=1

      SGLANG_FORCE_FUSED_OP_BACKEND=helion \
      SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \
      python -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 \
        --tokenizer-path meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 \
        --served-model-name external \
        --json-model-override-args '{"eos_token_id":[200001,200008]}' \
        --tp-size 4 \
        --ep-size 1 \
        --context-length 131072 \
        --max-running-requests 1 \
        --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
        --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
        --attention-backend trtllm_mha \
        --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
        --page-size 128 \
        --disable-flashinfer-autotune \
        --disable-prefill-cuda-graph \
        --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 1 \
        --reasoning-parser muse \
        --tool-call-parser muse \
        --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
        --speculative-draft-model-path RadixArk/Muse-Spark-Open-DFlash2 \
        --speculative-draft-attention-backend fa4 \
        --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 \
        --disaggregation-mode decode \
        --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
        --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
        --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --port 30002
<

Pair this worker with a compatible prefill worker using the same target
checkpoint, TP4, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--page-size 128`, and
`--served-model-name external`, with bootstrap port `8998`. Use the
|autoregressive-Meta-MuseSparkOpen-playground| PD router command with
`--model-id external` and the decode URL pointing to this worker on port
`30002`; send client requests to the router on port `8000`.

MiniMax-M2.5                      *sglang-autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5*

Deploy MiniMax-M2.5 with SGLang on NVIDIA, AMD, or Ascend A2, with an Ascend
A3 reference configuration.

                    *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-1-model-introduction*
1. MODEL INTRODUCTION

MiniMax-M2.5 https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5 is a powerful
language model developed by MiniMax, built for real-world productivity with
state-of-the-art performance across coding, reasoning, agentic tasks, and
tool use.

As the latest iteration in the MiniMax model series, MiniMax-M2.5 achieves
comprehensive enhancements across multiple domains. Details are as follows:

- Superior coding performance: Achieves 79.7 on Droid and 76.1 on OpenCode,
  surpassing Opus 4.6 (78.9 and 75.9 respectively). Strong results on
  SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench-pro, and
  Multi-SWE-bench.
- Advanced reasoning: Demonstrates strong performance on AIME25 and other
  reasoning benchmarks, with robust tool use during inference.
- More capable agents: Excels in agentic tasks including web browsing
  (BrowseComp, Wide Search), information retrieval (RISE), and complex tool
  use scenarios (Terminal Bench 2, MEWC, Finance Modeling).
- Real-world productivity: Designed for production-grade workloads with
  strong performance on practical coding, data analysis, and multi-step
  reasoning tasks.

For more details, please refer to the official MiniMax-M2.5 announcement
https://www.minimax.io/news/minimax-m25.

Ascend A3 prerequisites (unvalidated reference)

allocation labelled “1 NPU” is not a full node. The
|model-deployment-tutorials-minimax_m2_5-model-weights| is 4 cards / 8 dies
with 64 GB per die, while this preset requires all 16 dies.

  Note: ~

  This recipe is based on the upstream Ascend best practice. Hardware
  validation of the generated A3 cookbook command is pending; the reference
  accuracy and performance values below are not measurements of this recipe.
  The tested A2 selector is a separate low-concurrency configuration and
  does not validate the A3 preset.

*autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-3-4-ascend-a2-configuration-smoke-tested*
3.4 Ascend A2 configuration (smoke tested)

The A2 selector fixes TP=8, ModelSlim quantization, BF16,
`--context-length 4096`, and `--max-running-requests 1`. It uses prefill
chunks of 128, maximum prefill tokens of 4096, static memory fraction 0.96,
and `--max-total-tokens 4096`, and disables graph capture and radix cache.
No EAGLE3 draft model is required.

The `minimax` reasoning parser separated reasoning from answer content in
the tested runtime. The `minimax-m2` tool-call parser is configured, but
tool calling was not tested. The shared form displays a fixed 8-card count
and enabled parsers; these controls are read-only for this preset. The final
run allocated a 4096-token KV pool on all eight ranks and completed a
synthetic 3500-input/128-output request. This validates that request size on
this allocation, not every workload up to the configured limit. See section
5.4 for the earlier capacity failure and the final measurements. GPQA
accuracy, standardized throughput, and sustained stability remain unmeasured
for this single-request preset;
|autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-5-ascend-a2-performance-benchmark|
reports synthetic performance measurements using a separate server
configuration with concurrency up to 8.

4.2 Advanced Usage    *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-4-2-advanced-usage*

                  *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-4-2-1-reasoning-parser*
4.2.1 Reasoning Parser

MiniMax-M2.5 supports Thinking mode. Enable the reasoning parser during
deployment to separate the thinking and the content sections:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>bash
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5 \
      --tp 4 \
      --reasoning-parser minimax-append-think \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --mem-fraction-static 0.85
<
Streaming with Thinking Process

With `minimax-append-think`, the thinking content is wrapped in
`<think>...</think>` tags within the `content` field. You can parse these
tags on the client side to separate the thinking and content sections:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Enable streaming to see the thinking process in real-time
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "Solve this problem step by step: What is 15% of 240?"}
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
        max_tokens=2048,
        stream=True
    )

    # Process the stream, separating <think>...</think> from content
    in_think = False
    think_printed_header = False
    content_printed_header = False
    buffer = ""

    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices and len(chunk.choices) > 0:
            delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
            if delta.content:
                buffer += delta.content

                while buffer:
                    if in_think:
                        # Look for closing </think> tag
                        end_idx = buffer.find("</think>")
                        if end_idx != -1:
                            print(buffer[:end_idx], end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = buffer[end_idx + len("</think>"):]
                            in_think = False
                        else:
                            # Still in thinking, print what we have
                            print(buffer, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = ""
                    else:
                        # Look for opening <think> tag
                        start_idx = buffer.find("<think>")
                        if start_idx != -1:
                            # Print any content before <think>
                            before = buffer[:start_idx]
                            if before:
                                if not content_printed_header:
                                    print("=============== Content =================", flush=True)
                                    content_printed_header = True
                                print(before, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = buffer[start_idx + len("<think>"):]
                            in_think = True
                            if not think_printed_header:
                                print("=============== Thinking =================", flush=True)
                                think_printed_header = True
                        else:
                            # No <think> tag, print as content
                            if not content_printed_header and think_printed_header:
                                print("\n=============== Content =================", flush=True)
                                content_printed_header = True
                            print(buffer, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = ""

    print()
<
Output Example:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    =============== Thinking =================
    The user asks: "Solve this problem step by step: What is 15% of 240?" This is straightforward: 15% = 0.15; 0.15*240 = 36. So answer: 36. Provide step-by-step: convert percent to decimal, multiply.

    We need to obey policies. There's no policy violation. Just answer. Provide step by step. Should respond with solution.

    We can also mention alternative method: 15% = 15/100 = 3/20. Multiply 240 * 3/20 = (240/20)*3 = 12*3 = 36.

    Thus answer 36.

    We can add step-by-step. That's it.

    =============== Content =================

    **Step‑by‑step solution**

    1. **Convert the percent to a decimal**
       \[
       15\% = \frac{15}{100}=0.15
       \]

    2. **Multiply the decimal by the number**
       \[
       0.15 \times 240 = 36
       \]

    (You can also think of it as \(15\% = \frac{3}{20}\) and then \(240 \times \frac{3}{20}=12 \times 3 = 36\).)

    \[
    \boxed{36}
    \]
<
Note: The `minimax-append-think` reasoning parser embeds the thinking
process in `<think>...</think>` tags within the `content` field. The code
above parses these tags in real-time to display thinking and content
separately.

4.2.2 Tool Calling    *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-4-2-2-tool-calling*

MiniMax-M2.5 supports tool calling capabilities. Enable the tool call
parser:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>bash
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5 \
      --tp 4 \
      --tool-call-parser minimax-m2 \
      --reasoning-parser minimax-append-think \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --mem-fraction-static 0.85
<
Python Example:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Define available tools
    tools = [
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "get_weather",
                "description": "Get the current weather for a location",
                "parameters": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "location": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "The city name"
                        },
                        "unit": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                            "description": "Temperature unit"
                        }
                    },
                    "required": ["location"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]

    # Non-streaming request
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Beijing?"}
        ],
        tools=tools,
        temperature=0.7
    )

    message = response.choices[0].message

    # Check for tool calls
    if message.tool_calls:
        for tool_call in message.tool_calls:
            print(f"Tool Call: {tool_call.function.name}")
            print(f"   Arguments: {tool_call.function.arguments}")
    else:
        print(message.content)
<
Output Example:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    Tool Call: get_weather
       Arguments: {"location": "Beijing"}
<
Note: ~

- Tool calls are returned in `message.tool_calls` with the function name and
  arguments
- You can then execute the function and send the result back to continue the
  conversation

Handling Tool Call Results:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # After getting the tool call, execute the function
    def get_weather(location, unit="celsius"):
        # Your actual weather API call here
        return f"The weather in {location} is 22°{unit[0].upper()} and sunny."

    # Send tool result back to the model
    messages = [
        {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Beijing?"},
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": None,
            "tool_calls": [{
                "id": "call_123",
                "type": "function",
                "function": {
                    "name": "get_weather",
                    "arguments": '{"location": "Beijing", "unit": "celsius"}'
                }
            }]
        },
        {
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": "call_123",
            "content": get_weather("Beijing", "celsius")
        }
    ]

    final_response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.7
    )

    print(final_response.choices[0].message.content)
    # Output: "The weather in Beijing is currently 22°C and sunny."
<

        *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-4-3-verify-the-ascend-a3-service*
4.3 Verify the Ascend A3 service

Wait for the server to finish loading the weights and capturing graphs. Keep
the generated command running, then open another terminal in the same
container. The A3 preset listens on port 6688.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>bash
    curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 30 http://127.0.0.1:6688/health
    curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 30 http://127.0.0.1:6688/v1/models

    python3 - <<'PY'
    import json
    from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

    base = "http://127.0.0.1:6688"
    with urlopen(f"{base}/v1/models", timeout=30) as response:
        model = json.load(response)["data"][0]["id"]
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
        "temperature": 0,
        "max_tokens": 2048,
    }
    request = Request(
        f"{base}/v1/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urlopen(request, timeout=300) as response:
        result = json.load(response)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
    choice = result["choices"][0]
    assert (choice["message"].get("content") or "").strip(), "No final answer returned"
    assert choice["finish_reason"] != "length", "Increase the token budget and retry"
    PY
<
Check that the final answer identifies Paris. Repeat requests and check the
server logs for runtime errors. After any concurrent test, check `/health`
again. A successful HTTP response alone does not establish model accuracy;
use the evaluation below for that.

5. BENCHMARK                 *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-benchmark*

For Ascend A3, use

For Ascend A2,
|autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-4-ascend-a2-smoke-validation| records

|autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-5-ascend-a2-performance-benchmark|

measures 3500-input/1500-output requests, and
|autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-7-ascend-a2-fixed-50-question-gsm8k-regression|
records a fixed 50-question GSM8K deployment regression. No GPQA accuracy
result is reported here.

The benchmark sections below use industry-standard configurations for
comparable benchmark results; the A2 smoke record has a separate, limited
scope.

On September 22, 2026, the W8A8 main model completed loading, warm-up, and

`python/pyproject.toml` and a deleted `python/pyproject_npu.toml`; this was
not a clean source-build validation. An image digest and immutable model
revision were not captured, so this record is not a fully pinned environment

Timing includes HTTP/SSE processing and ends at the stream's `DONE` event.
First output means the first nonempty content or reasoning for chat, or the
first text or positive output-token count for native generation; it is not
the time to the final answer or a kernel timing. Completion counts include
reasoning and special tokens as reported by the server. Parser buffering and
chunks containing multiple tokens can affect observed timing. No cache flush
was performed. Each input length was measured once at concurrency 1, so
these results do not establish a latency percentile or saturation
throughput.

The final probe run completed and its post-run health check returned HTTP
200. Confirm startup KV allocation and actual request limits on your
allocation; the successful 3500-input/128-output probe does not establish
the full 4096-token boundary for every workload.

These checks establish simple chat functionality and the listed synthetic
request sizes. They do not establish GPQA accuracy, long-context answer
quality, sustained stability, tool calling, or performance under the A3
reference workload. This observed 8×32 GiB low-concurrency run does not
replace the upstream recommended hardware configuration.

           *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-5-2-reproduce-the-benchmark*
5.5.2 Reproduce the benchmark

Start the server above and wait for `/health` to return HTTP 200. Replace
the two model paths below with your container paths, using the same
tokenizer revision as the weights. Save the following as
`benchmark_minimax_a2.py` and run it from the tested SGLang environment. It
creates the synthetic data used here and runs the fixed suite, retaining
each command, log, and detailed JSONL result. It refuses to overwrite an
existing result and stops if a run fails validation.

[benchmark_minimax_a2.py]

[benchmark_minimax_a2.py]benchmark_minimax_a2.py

>python
    import json
    from pathlib import Path
    import subprocess
    import sys

    model = "/workspace/issue1215/model"
    tokenizer = "/workspace/issue1215/metadata"
    out = Path("minimax-a2-perf")
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    topics = [
        "gardening", "astronomy", "cooking", "geometry", "music", "weather",
        "transport", "ecology", "history", "software", "literature", "chemistry",
        "geography", "photography", "materials", "language",
    ]
    data = [{"id": f"synthetic-{i}", "conversations": [
        {"from": "human", "value": (
            f"Explain the basic principles of {topic}. Give a clear example and discuss its practical limitations. "
        ) * 8},
        {"from": "gpt", "value": "This is a synthetic performance workload, not a quality evaluation."},
    ]} for i, topic in enumerate(topics)]
    dataset = out / "synthetic-prompts.json"
    dataset.write_text(json.dumps(data), encoding="utf-8")
    cases = ([(128, 1, 4, 17)]
             + [(128, c, 8, s) for c in (4, 8) for s in (17, 29, 43)]
             + [(1024, 8, 8, s) for s in (17, 29, 43)])
    for length, concurrency, count, seed in cases:
        name = f"in{length}-out128-c{concurrency}-n{count}-seed{seed}"
        result = out / f"{name}.jsonl"
        if result.exists():
            raise RuntimeError(f"Refusing to overwrite {result}")
        command = [
            sys.executable, "-m", "sglang.benchmark.serving", "--backend", "sglang",
            "--base-url", "http://127.0.0.1:31216", "--model", model, "--tokenizer", tokenizer,
            "--dataset-name", "random", "--dataset-path", str(dataset),
            "--random-input-len", str(length), "--random-output-len", "128",
            "--random-range-ratio", "1", "--tokenize-prompt", "--num-prompts", str(count),
            "--max-concurrency", str(concurrency), "--request-rate", "inf",
            "--temperature", "0", "--seed", str(seed), "--warmup-requests", "1",
            "--flush-cache", "--output-details", "--disable-tqdm", "--output-file", str(result),
        ]
        (out / f"{name}.command.json").write_text(json.dumps(command, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
        with (out / f"{name}.log").open("w", encoding="utf-8") as log:
            subprocess.run(command, stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, check=True)
        rows = [json.loads(line) for line in result.read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
        if len(rows) != 1:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Expected exactly one result in {result}")
        row = rows[0]
        if not (row["completed"] == count
                and row["input_lens"] == [length] * count
                and row["output_lens"] == [128] * count
                and len(row["errors"]) == count and not any(row["errors"])):
            raise RuntimeError(f"Incomplete or mismatched run: inspect {result}")
        print(name, row["output_throughput"], flush=True)
<
Retain failed runs and missing-run records when reporting a reproduction; do
not summarize only successful seeds. Keep each run's mean and percentile
metrics separate. The synthetic data and performance measurements provide no
GPQA or other model-quality score.

*autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.5-5-7-ascend-a2-fixed-50-question-gsm8k-regression*
5.7 Ascend A2 fixed 50-question GSM8K regression

On September 24, 2026, a preselected 50-question deployment regression
completed with 49/50 correct (98%), zero capped outputs, zero
transport/protocol errors, and no missing or duplicate questions. This is a
bounded GSM8K test subset, not full GSM8K accuracy, an EvalScope result,
GPQA accuracy, or evidence of A3 parity.

The run used the same A2 hardware, W8A8 weights, and runtime as above. The
server used context 9216, maximum running requests 2, memory fraction 0.97,
and KV limit 16384; all other launch settings matched section 5.6. The
client submitted one request at a time to `/v1/chat/completions`, with
`temperature=1.0`, `max_tokens=6144`, and generation seed
`42 + original test row index`. The reasoning parser remained `minimax`;
scoring used only final answer content.

The protocol was frozen before an independent three-question pilot:

1. Use the MIT-licensed
   official GSM8K data at revision 3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c
   https://github.com/openai/grade-school-math/tree/3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c/grade_school_math/data.
   Take training rows 0--4 as five worked demonstrations.
2. Shuffle all 1319 test-row indices with Python
   `random.Random(20260924).shuffle`. Reserve the first three indices for
   the independent pilot and use the next 50, in order, for this regression.
   Do not include pilot answers in the result or select, replace, reorder,
   or drop questions based on observed answers.
3. Build a single user message by joining the five
   `Question: ...\nAnswer: ...` demonstrations with two newlines, then
   append the test question as `Question: ...\nAnswer:`. Preserve the
   training answers, including their worked solutions. Apply the deployed
   MiniMax chat template through the chat endpoint.
4. Before any generation, tokenize all 50 messages with the server and
   verify that each prompt plus the 6144-token output allowance fits context
   9216. Submit each frozen question exactly once, with a per-request wall
   limit of 1800 seconds. Stop new submissions on a transport/protocol
   error; do not retry or resume a failed run.
5. Parse only final content using the pinned runtime's last-number rule:
   remove commas, find matches of `-?\d+\.?\d*`, and parse the last match
   numerically. Compare it with the gold answer parsed the same way. A
   missing number, wrong answer, length cap, or transport/protocol error
   scores zero. Keep the denominator fixed at 50; report an incomplete run
   as incomplete rather than a full score.

The selection can be reconstructed without model access:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    import random

    indices = list(range(1319))
    random.Random(20260924).shuffle(indices)
    pilot_ids = indices[:3]       # Excluded from regression scoring.
    regression_ids = indices[3:53]
    assert len(set(regression_ids)) == 50
    assert not set(pilot_ids).intersection(regression_ids)
<

-------------------------------------------------  ---------------------------

Wrong final answers                                1
Length-capped responses                            0
Transport/protocol errors                          0
Completion-token range                             292--2507

All 50 prompts passed preflight. The client elapsed time, including
preflight, was 9444.598 seconds; it is not a per-request latency benchmark.
The downloaded run's 172 manifest entries passed hash verification, and
rescoring the preserved final answers with the declared parser reproduced
49/50. Preserve the frozen IDs, prompt hashes, parameters, every response,
and raw SSE when reproducing the regression. This result tests the declared

1. MODEL INTRODUCTION

MiniMax-M2.7 https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7 is MiniMax's
first model deeply participating in its own evolution. Built for real-world
productivity, M2.7 excels at building complex agent harnesses and completing
highly elaborate productivity tasks, leveraging Agent Teams, complex Skills,
and dynamic tool search.

Key highlights:

- Model Self-Evolution: During development, M2.7 updates its own memory,
  builds complex skills for RL experiments, and improves its own learning
  process. An internal version autonomously optimized a programming scaffold
  over 100+ rounds, achieving a 30% performance improvement. On MLE Bench
  Lite, M2.7 achieved a 66.6% medal rate.
- Professional Software Engineering: Delivers outstanding real-world
  programming capabilities. On SWE-Pro, M2.7 achieved 56.22%, with strong
  results on SWE Multilingual (76.5) and Multi SWE Bench (52.7). On Terminal
  Bench 2 (57.0%) and NL2Repo (39.8%), M2.7 demonstrates deep understanding
  of complex engineering systems.
- Professional Work: Achieved an ELO score of 1495 on GDPval-AA (highest
  among open-source models). On Toolathon, M2.7 reached 46.3% accuracy
  (global top tier).
- Native Agent Teams: Supports multi-agent collaboration with stable role
  identity and autonomous decision-making.

For more details, see the official MiniMax-M2.7 blog post
https://www.minimax.io/news/minimax-m27-en.

4.2 Advanced Usage    *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.7-4-2-advanced-usage*

                  *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.7-4-2-1-reasoning-parser*
4.2.1 Reasoning Parser

MiniMax-M2.7 supports Thinking mode. Enable the reasoning parser during
deployment to separate the thinking and the content sections:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>bash
    sglang serve \
      --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7 \
      --tp 4 \
      --reasoning-parser minimax-append-think \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --mem-fraction-static 0.85
<
Streaming with Thinking Process

With `minimax-append-think`, the thinking content is wrapped in
`<think>...</think>` tags within the `content` field. You can parse these
tags on the client side to separate the thinking and content sections:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Enable streaming to see the thinking process in real-time
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "Solve this problem step by step: What is 15% of 240?"}
        ],
        max_tokens=2048,
        stream=True
    )

    # Process the stream, separating <think>...</think> from content
    in_think = False
    think_printed_header = False
    content_printed_header = False
    buffer = ""

    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices and len(chunk.choices) > 0:
            delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
            if delta.content:
                buffer += delta.content

                while buffer:
                    if in_think:
                        # Look for closing </think> tag
                        end_idx = buffer.find("</think>")
                        if end_idx != -1:
                            print(buffer[:end_idx], end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = buffer[end_idx + len("</think>"):]
                            in_think = False
                        else:
                            # Still in thinking, print what we have
                            print(buffer, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = ""
                    else:
                        # Look for opening <think> tag
                        start_idx = buffer.find("<think>")
                        if start_idx != -1:
                            # Print any content before <think>
                            before = buffer[:start_idx]
                            if before:
                                if not content_printed_header:
                                    print("=============== Content =================", flush=True)
                                    content_printed_header = True
                                print(before, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = buffer[start_idx + len("<think>"):]
                            in_think = True
                            if not think_printed_header:
                                print("=============== Thinking =================", flush=True)
                                think_printed_header = True
                        else:
                            # No <think> tag, print as content
                            if not content_printed_header and think_printed_header:
                                print("\n=============== Content =================", flush=True)
                                content_printed_header = True
                            print(buffer, end="", flush=True)
                            buffer = ""

    print()
<
Output Example:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    =============== Thinking =================
    The user asks: "Solve this problem step by step: What is 15% of 240?" Straightforward. Provide solution: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15. Multiply 240 * 0.15 = 36. Show steps. So answer: 36. Provide explanation.

    But also ensure we follow any policy? No issues. Just straightforward.

    I'll provide a step-by-step solution.

    Also could show fraction: 15% = 15/100 = 3/20, multiply 240 * 3/20 = (240/20)*3 = 12*3 = 36.

    Yes. Provide final answer. Also show verification: 10% of 240 is 24, 5% is 12, total 36.

    All good.

    =============== Content =================

    **Step‑by‑step solution**

    1. **Convert the percent to a decimal (or a fraction).**

       15% = 15/100 = 0.15 = 3/20

    2. **Multiply the original number (240) by this decimal/fraction.**

       Using the decimal:
       240 × 0.15 = 36

       Or using the fraction:
       240 × 3/20 = (240/20) × 3 = 12 × 3 = 36

    3. **Result:**

       15% of 240 = **36**

    *Check:*
    - 10% of 240 = 24
    - 5% of 240 = 12
    - Adding them: 24 + 12 = 36, which matches the calculation.
<
Note: The `minimax-append-think` reasoning parser embeds the thinking
process in `<think>...</think>` tags within the `content` field. The code
above parses these tags in real-time to display thinking and content
separately.

4.2.2 Tool Calling    *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2.7-4-2-2-tool-calling*

MiniMax-M2.7 supports tool calling capabilities. Enable the tool call
parser:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>bash
    sglang serve \
      --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7 \
      --tp 4 \
      --tool-call-parser minimax-m2 \
      --reasoning-parser minimax-append-think \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --mem-fraction-static 0.85
<
Python Example:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Define available tools
    tools = [
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "get_weather",
                "description": "Get the current weather for a location",
                "parameters": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "location": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "The city name"
                        },
                        "unit": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                            "description": "Temperature unit"
                        }
                    },
                    "required": ["location"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]

    # Non-streaming request
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Beijing?"}
        ],
        tools=tools
    )

    message = response.choices[0].message

    # Check for tool calls
    if message.tool_calls:
        for tool_call in message.tool_calls:
            print(f"Tool Call: {tool_call.function.name}")
            print(f"   Arguments: {tool_call.function.arguments}")
    else:
        print(message.content)
<
Output Example:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    Tool Call: get_weather
       Arguments: {"location": "Beijing"}
<
Handling Tool Call Results:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # After getting the tool call, execute the function
    def get_weather(location, unit="celsius"):
        # Your actual weather API call here
        return f"The weather in {location} is 22°{unit[0].upper()} and sunny."

    # Send tool result back to the model
    messages = [
        {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Beijing?"},
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": None,
            "tool_calls": [{
                "id": "call_123",
                "type": "function",
                "function": {
                    "name": "get_weather",
                    "arguments": '{"location": "Beijing", "unit": "celsius"}'
                }
            }]
        },
        {
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": "call_123",
            "content": get_weather("Beijing", "celsius")
        }
    ]

    final_response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7",
        messages=messages
    )

    print(final_response.choices[0].message.content)
<
Output Example:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    The weather in Beijing is currently 22°C and sunny.
<

MiniMax-M2                          *sglang-autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2*

1. MODEL INTRODUCTION *autoregressive-MiniMax-MiniMax-M2-1-model-introduction*

MiniMax-M2 https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2 is a compact, fast,
and cost-effective MoE model (230 billion total parameters with 10 billion
active parameters) built for elite performance in coding and agentic tasks,
all while maintaining powerful general intelligence.

This generation delivers comprehensive upgrades across the board:

- Superior Intelligence: MiniMax-M2 demonstrates highly competitive general
  intelligence across mathematics, science, instruction following, coding,
  and agentic tool use in Artificial Analysis
  https://artificialanalysis.ai/. Its composite score ranks #1 among
  open-source models globally.
- Advanced Coding: Engineered for end-to-end developer workflows, MiniMax-M2
  excels at multi-file edits, coding-run-fix loops, and test-validated
  repairs. Strong performance on Terminal-Bench and (Multi-)SWE-Bench--style
  tasks demonstrates practical effectiveness in terminals, IDEs, and CI
  across languages.
- Agent Performance: MiniMax-M2 plans and executes complex, long-horizon
  toolchains across shell, browser, retrieval, and code runners. In
  BrowseComp-style evaluations, it consistently locates hard-to-surface
  sources, maintains evidence traceable, and gracefully recovers from flaky
  steps.
- Efficient Design: With 10 billion activated parameters (230 billion in
  total), MiniMax-M2 delivers lower latency, lower cost, and higher
  throughput for interactive agents and batched sampling---perfectly aligned
  with the shift toward highly deployable models that still shine on coding
  and agentic tasks.

For more details, please refer to the official Minimax GitHub Repository
https://github.com/MiniMax-AI.

Test Code:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Enable streaming to see the thinking process in real-time
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "Solve this problem step by step: What is 15% of 240?"}
        ],
        temperature=0.6,
        max_tokens=2048,
        stream=True
    )

    # Process the stream
    has_thinking = False
    has_answer = False
    thinking_started = False

    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices and len(chunk.choices) > 0:
            delta = chunk.choices[0].delta

            # Print thinking process
            if hasattr(delta, 'reasoning_content') and delta.reasoning_content:
                if not thinking_started:
                    print("=============== Thinking =================", flush=True)
                    thinking_started = True
                has_thinking = True
                print(delta.reasoning_content, end="", flush=True)

            # Print answer content
            if delta.content:
                # Close thinking section and add content header
                if has_thinking and not has_answer:
                    print("\n=============== Content =================", flush=True)
                    has_answer = True
                print(delta.content, end="", flush=True)

    print()

    To find a percentage of a number, I multiply the number by the percentage divided by 100. So, 15% is 15/100, which simplifies to 0.15.

    Therefore, 15% of 240 is 240 times 0.15.

    Let me calculate that: 240 × 0.15.

    I can break it down: 240 × 0.15 = 240 × (15/100) = (240 × 15) / 100.

    Now, 240 × 15. 200 × 15 = 3000, and 40 × 15 = 600, so total 3000 + 600 = 3600.

    Then, divide by 100: 3600 / 100 = 36.

    So, 15% of 240 is 36.

    I should confirm this with another method. For example, 10% of 240 is 24, and 5% is half of that, which is 12. Then 15% is 10% + 5% = 24 + 12 = 36. Same answer.

    Or, using fractions: 15% = 3/20, so 240 × 3/20 = (240 / 20) × 3 = 12 × 3 = 36.

    All methods confirm it's 36.

    Step 3: Multiply the number by the decimal: 240 × 0.15.

Test Code:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
        api_key="EMPTY"
    )

    # Define available tools
    tools = [
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "get_weather",
                "description": "Get the current weather for a location",
                "parameters": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "location": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "The city name"
                        },
                        "unit": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                            "description": "Temperature unit"
                        }
                    },
                    "required": ["location"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]

    # Make request with streaming to see thinking process
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Beijing?"}
        ],
        tools=tools,
        temperature=0.7,
        stream=True
    )

    # Process streaming response
    thinking_started = False
    has_thinking = False
    tool_calls_accumulator = {}

    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices and len(chunk.choices) > 0:
            delta = chunk.choices[0].delta

            # Print thinking process
            if hasattr(delta, 'reasoning_content') and delta.reasoning_content:
                if not thinking_started:
                    print("=============== Thinking =================", flush=True)
                    thinking_started = True
                has_thinking = True
                print(delta.reasoning_content, end="", flush=True)

            # Accumulate tool calls
            if hasattr(delta, 'tool_calls') and delta.tool_calls:
                # Close thinking section if needed
                if has_thinking and thinking_started:
                    print("\n=============== Content =================\n", flush=True)
                    thinking_started = False

                for tool_call in delta.tool_calls:
                    index = tool_call.index
                    if index not in tool_calls_accumulator:
                        tool_calls_accumulator[index] = {
                            'name': None,
                            'arguments': ''
                        }

                    if tool_call.function:
                        if tool_call.function.name:
                            tool_calls_accumulator[index]['name'] = tool_call.function.name
                        if tool_call.function.arguments:
                            tool_calls_accumulator[index]['arguments'] += tool_call.function.arguments

            # Print content
            if delta.content:
                print(delta.content, end="", flush=True)

    # Print accumulated tool calls
    for index, tool_call in sorted(tool_calls_accumulator.items()):
        print(f"🔧 Tool Call: {tool_call['name']}")
        print(f"   Arguments: {tool_call['arguments']}")

    print()
<
Output Example:

[Output]Output

    Alright, the user is asking about the weather in Beijing. This is a straightforward request that I can help with using the get_weather tool that's available to me.

    Let me think about what I need to do here. The user wants to know the current weather conditions in Beijing, which is the capital city of China. To provide this information, I need to use the get_weather tool that's been provided to me.

    Looking at the tool's parameters, I can see it requires:
    1. location - which is required and should be a string representing the city name
    2. unit - which is optional and can be either "celsius" or "fahrenheit"

    For the location parameter, I'll use "Beijing" since that's what the user asked about.

    For the unit parameter, the user didn't specify their preference between celsius and fahrenheit. Since Beijing is in China, which primarily uses celsius, and celsius is the more standard unit internationally, I'll default to celsius. If the user wants the temperature in fahrenheit instead, they can ask in a follow-up message and I can provide that information.

    So I need to make a tool call to get_weather with the following parameters:
    - location: "Beijing"
    - unit: "celsius"

    This should return the current weather information for Beijing, which I can then share with the user. I'll format my response using the required XML tags for tool calls as specified in my instructions.
    </think>
